question: What are semantic HTML elements and why do they matter?
short: Semantic elements (`<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<article>`, `<section>`, `<aside>`, `<footer>`) describe the meaning of content rather than its appearance, improving accessibility, SEO, and maintainability.
answer:
**Semantic elements** convey the *meaning and role* of their content to browsers, assistive technologies, and search engines, unlike generic containers like `<div>`/`<span>` which carry no meaning.

**Why they matter:**
- **Accessibility** - Many map to ARIA *landmarks* (`<nav>` -> `navigation`, `<main>` -> `main`, `<aside>` -> `complementary`), letting screen-reader users jump directly between regions.
- **SEO** - Search engines infer content hierarchy and importance from structure.
- **Maintainability** - Self-documenting markup is easier to read than a sea of `<div>`s.

**Common landmarks:**
- `<header>` - introductory content / banner.
- `<nav>` - major navigation block.
- `<main>` - the single primary content region (one per page).
- `<article>` - self-contained, independently distributable content (a blog post, comment, card).
- `<section>` - a thematic grouping, usually with a heading.
- `<aside>` - tangential content (sidebars, pull quotes).
- `<footer>` - footer for its nearest sectioning ancestor.

**Rule of thumb:** use `<article>` when the content would make sense on its own (e.g. in an RSS feed); use `<section>` to group related content under a heading.

question: What is the difference between <section>, <article>, and <div>?
short: `<article>` is self-contained, reusable content; `<section>` is a thematic group of related content (usually with a heading); `<div>` is a meaningless generic container used only for styling or scripting hooks.
answer:
These three are frequently confused:

- **`<article>`** - independently distributable, self-contained content that still makes sense out of context (a news story, forum post, product card, comment). You can nest articles (e.g. comments inside a post article).
- **`<section>`** - a thematic grouping of content, typically introduced by a heading. Use it when content belongs together but is *not* independently meaningful. If the only reason is styling, it should not be a `<section>`.
- **`<div>`** - a *non-semantic* generic block container. It has no meaning and exposes no landmark; use it purely as a styling/layout/JS hook.

**Decision guide:** Does the content stand alone and could be syndicated? -> `<article>`. Is it a meaningful thematic chunk with a heading? -> `<section>`. Neither, just need a box? -> `<div>`.

question: What is the DOCTYPE and what is quirks mode?
short: `<!DOCTYPE html>` tells the browser to use standards mode for consistent, spec-compliant rendering. Omitting or using an invalid doctype triggers quirks mode, which emulates legacy 1990s browser bugs.
answer:
The **DOCTYPE** is the first line of an HTML document. The modern `<!DOCTYPE html>` is not a tag and contains no version - it simply switches the browser into **standards mode**.

**The three rendering modes:**
- **Standards (no-quirks) mode** - the browser follows the current HTML/CSS specs. This is what you want.
- **Quirks mode** - triggered by a missing/invalid doctype; the browser mimics non-standard behavior of old browsers for backward compatibility.
- **Limited-quirks (almost standards) mode** - mostly standards, with a few legacy quirks (notably around inline image box height in table cells).

**Classic quirks-mode differences:**
- The **box model** reverts to the old IE model (padding/border counted inside `width`).
- Different handling of `line-height`, percentages, and image spacing.

**Takeaway:** Always include `<!DOCTYPE html>` to guarantee standards mode and avoid subtle cross-browser layout bugs.

question: What is the difference between the async and defer attributes on a <script>?
short: Both download the script without blocking HTML parsing. `async` runs as soon as it loads (order not guaranteed); `defer` waits until parsing finishes and preserves source order, running just before `DOMContentLoaded`.
answer:
By default a `<script>` is **parser-blocking**: HTML parsing pauses while the script downloads and executes. `async` and `defer` (valid only on external scripts with `src`) avoid blocking the download.

| Attribute | Download | Execution | Order preserved? |
|-----------|----------|-----------|------------------|
| (none) | blocks parsing | immediately, blocks parsing | yes |
| `async` | parallel, non-blocking | **as soon as downloaded**, may interrupt parsing | **no** |
| `defer` | parallel, non-blocking | **after parsing completes**, before `DOMContentLoaded` | **yes** |

**When to use which:**
- **`defer`** - for scripts that depend on the DOM or on each other (most app/bundle code). Safe default.
- **`async`** - for independent, order-agnostic scripts like analytics or ad tags.
- **Modules** (`<script type="module">`) are deferred by default.

Note: `async` execution timing is unpredictable relative to DOM readiness, which is why ordered dependencies should use `defer`.
code:
<!-- Runs after HTML is parsed, in order -->
<script src="app.js" defer></script>

<!-- Independent, runs whenever it arrives -->
<script src="analytics.js" async></script>

question: What are data-* attributes and when should you use them?
short: `data-*` attributes store custom private data on an element. They are read/written via `element.dataset` (or `getAttribute`) and are meant for app data, not styling hooks or accessibility info.
answer:
**`data-*` attributes** are a standard way to attach custom, application-specific data to HTML elements without abusing non-standard attributes or class names.

**Access from JavaScript** via the `dataset` property, where `data-user-id` becomes `dataset.userId` (kebab-case maps to camelCase). You can also use `getAttribute('data-user-id')`.

**Good uses:**
- Passing IDs/config from server-rendered HTML to JS (e.g. `data-product-id`).
- State flags for JS behavior or CSS via attribute selectors (`[data-state="open"]`).

**Avoid using them for:**
- Data that has a proper attribute (use `value`, `href`, `title`, etc. instead).
- **Accessibility** - assistive tech does not read `data-*`; use ARIA/visible text.
- Large datasets or as a database substitute.
code:
<button data-product-id="42" data-in-stock="true">Buy</button>

<script>
  const btn = document.querySelector('button');
  btn.dataset.productId; // "42"
  btn.dataset.inStock;   // "true" (always a string)
</script>

question: What is the difference between localStorage, sessionStorage, and cookies?
short: All store data on the client. localStorage persists indefinitely; sessionStorage lasts for one tab session. Both are JS-only (~5-10MB). Cookies are smaller (~4KB) and sent with every HTTP request, making them suited to server-side session state.
answer:
| Feature | localStorage | sessionStorage | Cookies |
|---------|--------------|----------------|---------|
| Capacity | ~5-10 MB | ~5-10 MB | ~4 KB |
| Lifetime | until cleared | until tab closes | `Expires`/`Max-Age` |
| Scope | per origin | per origin + per tab | per domain/path |
| Sent to server | no | no | **yes, every request** |
| API | `localStorage` | `sessionStorage` | `document.cookie` / headers |

**When to use each:**
- **localStorage** - persistent client-only data: theme, UI preferences, non-sensitive caches.
- **sessionStorage** - data scoped to a single tab/visit: multi-step form progress, scroll state.
- **Cookies** - data the **server** needs on each request, especially auth/session tokens. Secure them with `HttpOnly` (blocks JS access, mitigates XSS), `Secure` (HTTPS only), and `SameSite` (mitigates CSRF).

**Security:** Web Storage is always accessible to JS, so it is vulnerable to XSS; never store secrets there. `HttpOnly` cookies are the safer place for session tokens.

question: What are meta tags and which ones matter for SEO and rendering?
short: `<meta>` tags supply metadata about the document (charset, viewport, description) in the `<head>`. Key ones include charset, viewport for responsiveness, description for search snippets, and robots for crawler control.
answer:
**`<meta>`** elements provide machine-readable metadata that doesn't appear on the page itself but influences rendering, indexing, and how the page is shared.

**Critical for rendering:**
- `<meta charset="utf-8">` - declares character encoding; should be first in `<head>`.
- `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` - essential for responsive/mobile layout.

**Important for SEO/sharing:**
- `<meta name="description">` - the snippet search engines often show (does not directly affect ranking but affects click-through).
- `<meta name="robots" content="index, follow">` - controls crawling/indexing (`noindex`, `nofollow`).
- `<title>` - not a meta tag, but the single most important on-page SEO/UX signal.
- `<link rel="canonical">` - declares the preferred URL to avoid duplicate-content issues.

**Note:** The `keywords` meta tag is obsolete - major search engines ignore it.
code:
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Concise, Unique Page Title</title>
  <meta name="description" content="A 150-160 char summary for search results.">
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/page">
</head>

question: What is Open Graph and why is it used?
short: Open Graph (`og:`) meta tags let you control how a page appears when shared on social platforms - the title, description, and preview image - producing rich link previews instead of bare URLs.
answer:
**Open Graph Protocol** is a set of `<meta property="og:*">` tags (originally from Facebook) that social networks and chat apps read to build a **rich preview card** when your link is shared.

**Core tags:**
- `og:title` - title shown on the card (can differ from `<title>`).
- `og:description` - the preview blurb.
- `og:image` - the preview thumbnail (specify an absolute URL; recommend ~1200x630).
- `og:url` - the canonical URL of the page.
- `og:type` - e.g. `website`, `article`.

**Twitter/X** has a parallel set (`twitter:card`, `twitter:image`) but falls back to Open Graph when those are absent.

**Why it matters:** Without these tags, shared links render as plain text/URLs; with them, links get attractive cards that improve click-through and brand presentation. They have no effect on the page's own rendering.
code:
<meta property="og:title" content="My Article">
<meta property="og:description" content="Short, compelling summary.">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/cover.png">
<meta property="og:url" content="https://example.com/article">
<meta property="og:type" content="article">

question: What is ARIA and when should you use it?
short: ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) adds roles, states, and properties to convey semantics to assistive tech when native HTML can't. Use it only to fill genuine gaps - native elements are always preferred.
answer:
**ARIA** is a set of attributes that describe the **role**, **state**, and **properties** of UI to assistive technologies, mainly for custom or dynamic widgets where native HTML falls short.

**Three categories:**
- **Roles** - what an element *is*: `role="tab"`, `role="dialog"`, `role="alert"`.
- **States** - dynamic conditions: `aria-expanded`, `aria-checked`, `aria-disabled`.
- **Properties** - relationships/labels: `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-controls`.

**The rules of ARIA:**
1. **Don't use ARIA if a native element/attribute provides the semantics** (use `<button>`, not `<div role="button">`).
2. **Don't change native semantics** unless you must.
3. All interactive ARIA controls must be **keyboard usable**.
4. **Don't use `role="presentation"` or `aria-hidden="true"` on focusable elements.**

**Key point:** ARIA changes only *how things are announced* - it adds **no behavior**. You must wire up keyboard handling and state updates yourself. Hence: *no ARIA is better than bad ARIA.*

Useful live-region attributes: `aria-live="polite"`/`"assertive"` announce dynamic content changes (toasts, validation messages).

question: Why is the alt attribute important and how should you write it?
short: `alt` provides a text alternative for images: read by screen readers, shown if the image fails to load, and used by search engines. Describe the image's purpose; use empty `alt=""` for purely decorative images.
answer: The **`alt`** attribute on `` is the image's text alternative and is required for accessible, robust pages. **It serves three roles:** 1. **Accessibility** - screen readers announce it; without it they may read the filename or skip the image. 2. **Fallback** - displayed if the image fails to load. 3. **SEO** - search engines use it to understand and index images. **How to write good alt text:** - Describe the **purpose/meaning** in context, not every pixel. For a logo link: `alt="Acme - home"`. - Keep it concise; don't start with "image of" (the role is already known). - **Decorative images** that add no information should use **empty alt** (`alt=""`) so screen readers skip them. Omitting `alt` entirely is *not* the same - that can cause the filename to be read. - For images conveying complex data (charts), provide a longer description nearby or via `aria-describedby`.

question: Why are <label> elements important and how do you associate them with inputs?
short: A `<label>` gives a form control an accessible name and a larger click target. Associate it via `for`/`id` matching, or by wrapping the input inside the label.
answer:
A **`<label>`** ties human-readable text to a form control, which is essential for usability and accessibility.

**Benefits:**
- Screen readers announce the label when the control is focused (provides its *accessible name*).
- Clicking/tapping the label focuses or toggles the control - a bigger hit area, important for checkboxes/radios and touch.

**Two ways to associate:**
1. **Explicit** - `<label for="email">` matches `<input id="email">`. Preferred; works even when not adjacent.
2. **Implicit** - wrap the input inside the label.

**Related grouping:** wrap a set of related controls (e.g. radio options) in a **`<fieldset>`** with a **`<legend>`** to give the group an accessible name. Placeholder text is *not* a substitute for a label - it disappears on input and has poor contrast/AT support.
code:
<!-- Explicit (preferred) -->
<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email" name="email">

<!-- Grouped controls -->
<fieldset>
  <legend>Shipping speed</legend>
  <label><input type="radio" name="speed" value="std"> Standard</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="speed" value="exp"> Express</label>
</fieldset>

question: What HTML5 input types and native validation features exist, and why use them?
short: HTML5 added input types like email, url, number, date, tel, and color, plus validation attributes (required, pattern, min/max, type). They give appropriate keyboards, built-in validation, and accessible error messaging for free.
answer:
HTML5 expanded `<input type>` well beyond `text`, and added **native (constraint) validation** so common checks need no JavaScript.

**Useful input types:** `email`, `url`, `tel`, `number`, `range`, `date`/`time`/`datetime-local`, `color`, `search`, `password`, `file`. On mobile these trigger the **appropriate on-screen keyboard** and pickers.

**Validation attributes:**
- `required` - field must be filled.
- `type="email"`/`"url"` - format checking.
- `pattern="..."` - regex constraint.
- `min`, `max`, `step` - numeric/date bounds.
- `minlength`, `maxlength` - length bounds.

**Why use it:**
- **Free, accessible** validation UI and messages, before any JS loads.
- Style states with CSS pseudo-classes `:valid`, `:invalid`, `:required`.
- Hook into the **Constraint Validation API** (`checkValidity()`, `setCustomValidity()`) for custom messages.

**Caveat:** client-side validation is for UX only - **always re-validate on the server**, since it can be bypassed.
code:
<form>
  <input type="email" required placeholder="you@site.com">
  <input type="number" min="1" max="10" step="1" required>
  <input type="text" pattern="[A-Za-z]{3,}" title="Letters only, 3+">
  <button>Submit</button>
</form>

question: What is the difference between GET and POST methods on a form?
short: GET appends form data to the URL as a query string - good for idempotent, bookmarkable, non-sensitive reads. POST sends data in the request body - used for changes, large payloads, or sensitive data.
answer:
The form `method` attribute controls how submitted data is sent.

**GET:**
- Data is appended to the URL as a **query string** (`?q=...&page=2`).
- **Bookmarkable / shareable**, cached, and shown in browser history.
- Limited length; **never** for passwords or sensitive data (it leaks into URLs, logs, history).
- Semantically for **safe, idempotent reads** (search, filters).

**POST:**
- Data is sent in the **request body**, not the URL.
- No practical size limit; supports file uploads (`enctype="multipart/form-data"`).
- Not cached or bookmarked; re-submitting may prompt the user.
- Semantically for actions that **change state** (create, update, delete) and for sensitive data.

**Note:** POST is not encryption - only **HTTPS** protects data in transit. The choice is about semantics and where data travels, not security by itself.
code:
<form action="/search" method="get">...</form>   <!-- read -->
<form action="/users" method="post">...</form>   <!-- create -->

question: How do srcset/sizes and the <picture> element enable responsive images?
short: `srcset`+`sizes` let the browser pick the best-resolution image for the viewport/DPR (resolution switching). `<picture>` with `<source media>` lets you swap entirely different images or formats (art direction).
answer: Two complementary mechanisms serve the right image to each device, saving bandwidth and improving performance. **1. `srcset` + `sizes` (resolution switching)** - same image, different sizes; the **browser chooses**. - `srcset` lists candidate files with width descriptors (`480w`, `800w`). - `sizes` tells the browser how wide the image will *render* at various breakpoints, so it can pick the smallest sufficient file (also accounts for device pixel ratio). **2. `` + `` (art direction & format negotiation)** - *you* control which image is used. - Use `media` queries to serve a cropped/different image at different breakpoints. - Use `type` to offer modern formats (AVIF/WebP) with a fallback `` for older browsers. - The `` inside `` is required - it's the fallback and carries `alt`. **Key distinction:** `srcset`/`sizes` = browser optimizes the *same* image; `` = developer dictates *different* images/formats.

question: What is an <iframe> and how does the sandbox attribute secure it?
short: An `<iframe>` embeds another HTML document inside the current page. The `sandbox` attribute restricts the embedded content (scripts, forms, popups, same-origin access), re-granting capabilities only via explicit tokens.
answer:
An **`<iframe>`** embeds an independent browsing context (another document) within the page - used for third-party widgets, maps, videos, payment forms, etc.

**Risks:** embedded content can run scripts, submit forms, trigger navigation, or open popups. The **`sandbox`** attribute applies a strict default-deny policy.

- **`sandbox` with no value** - maximum restriction: no scripts, no forms, no popups, treated as a unique opaque origin (no same-origin access), no top-level navigation.
- **Re-enable selectively** with space-separated tokens:
  - `allow-scripts` - permit JavaScript.
  - `allow-forms` - permit form submission.
  - `allow-same-origin` - keep its real origin.
  - `allow-popups`, `allow-top-navigation`, etc.

**Caution:** combining `allow-scripts` **and** `allow-same-origin` lets the frame remove its own sandboxing, so avoid that pairing for untrusted content.

**Related security attributes:** `referrerpolicy`, `loading="lazy"`, and `allow` (Permissions Policy) for features like camera/fullscreen. Server-side, `X-Frame-Options`/`frame-ancestors` (CSP) control whether *your* page can be framed by others (clickjacking defense).
code:
<iframe src="https://widget.example.com"
        sandbox="allow-scripts allow-forms"
        loading="lazy"
        title="Embedded widget"></iframe>

question: What is the difference between <canvas> and SVG?
short: Canvas is a raster, pixel-based bitmap drawn imperatively via JS (no DOM for shapes) - great for many objects and pixel manipulation. SVG is vector, resolution-independent, and DOM-based - great for scalable, interactive, accessible graphics.
answer:
Both render graphics in the browser but differ fundamentally.

**`<canvas>` (raster / immediate mode):**
- A pixel bitmap you draw onto with the **2D/WebGL JavaScript API**.
- Shapes are **not** in the DOM - once drawn, they're just pixels (no per-shape events, must redraw to change).
- **Resolution-dependent** - scaling up blurs/pixelates.
- Best for: games, charts with thousands of points, image/video processing, real-time pixel work.

**SVG (vector / retained mode):**
- XML markup; each shape is a **DOM element** you can style with CSS and attach event listeners to.
- **Resolution-independent** - scales crisply at any size/DPI.
- **Accessible** (can include `<title>`/`<desc>`, ARIA) and easily animated/styled.
- Best for: icons, logos, diagrams, interactive charts, anything that must scale or be styled.

**Rule of thumb:** few, interactive, scalable elements -> **SVG**; many objects or pixel-level/high-frequency rendering -> **canvas** (DOM overhead would make SVG slow).
code:
<!-- SVG: vector, in the DOM, styleable -->
<svg viewBox="0 0 100 100" role="img" aria-label="Circle">
  <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="tomato"/>
</svg>

<!-- Canvas: pixels drawn via JS -->
<canvas id="c" width="100" height="100"></canvas>
<script>
  const ctx = document.getElementById('c').getContext('2d');
  ctx.fillStyle = 'tomato';
  ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(50, 50, 40, 0, Math.PI*2); ctx.fill();
</script>

question: What is the DOM and how does it relate to HTML?
short: The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's live, in-memory tree representation of a parsed HTML document. HTML is the static source text; the DOM is the dynamic object model that JS reads and mutates.
answer:
The **DOM (Document Object Model)** is a **language-neutral, tree-structured object representation** of a document that the browser builds while parsing the HTML. Each element, attribute, and text node becomes an object (a node) that scripts can query and manipulate.

**HTML vs DOM:**
- **HTML** is the *static source* - the markup you write/send.
- The browser *parses* it into the **DOM tree** - a live structure in memory.
- They can diverge: the browser **fixes invalid markup**, injects implied elements (e.g. `<tbody>`), and JS can add/remove/modify nodes after load. So "View Source" (original HTML) can differ from "Inspect" (current DOM).

**Why it matters:**
- JS uses DOM APIs (`getElementById`, `querySelector`, `createElement`, `addEventListener`) to read and change the page dynamically.
- DOM manipulation can be expensive; reflows/repaints are why frameworks (React's virtual DOM, etc.) batch updates.
- The **CSSOM** (styles) combines with the DOM into the **render tree** the browser paints.

question: What belongs in <head> versus <body>?
short: `<head>` holds metadata not rendered in the page - title, charset, viewport, links to CSS, scripts, SEO/social tags. `<body>` holds the visible, rendered content the user sees and interacts with.
answer:
Every HTML document splits into two top-level sections inside `<html>`:

**`<head>` - metadata and resources (not rendered as content):**
- `<title>` - tab/bookmark/SEO title.
- `<meta>` - charset, viewport, description, robots, Open Graph.
- `<link>` - stylesheets, `canonical`, `preconnect`/`preload`, favicons.
- `<script>` - though often deferred or placed at the end of `<body>`.
- `<style>` - inline CSS.

**`<body>` - the visible document:**
- All structural/semantic content: headings, text, images, forms, links, etc.

**Why the split matters:**
- `<meta charset>` must appear early in `<head>` so the browser decodes text correctly.
- Render-blocking CSS in `<head>` avoids a flash of unstyled content; scripts are commonly deferred so they don't block parsing.
- Resource hints (`preconnect`, `preload`, `dns-prefetch`) in `<head>` improve load performance.
